title: Eight Weeks on the Long Road Back
subtitle: An eight week plan from James Bell for the one who can't stop drinking or using. Stopping safely with a doctor, one person who knows, the hardest hour, shame brought into the light, and a life to live toward.
intro:
This is an eight week plan for the person who can't stop drinking or using, who has promised that this was the last time, meant it, and watched the promise give way by evening. Each week holds one focus, one small daily practice, one thing to read, one tool to use, and one honest question. It begins with stopping safely and telling one person the whole truth, then moves through the hour and the places where resolve tends to break, the shame that keeps it hidden, and what the substance has been quieting, toward confession and company, a body given time to heal, and a life with something to live toward. You don't have to share my faith for these practices to help. If you're reading for someone you love who drinks or uses, start instead with the care page linked in week one; its section called If you're helping someone was written for you.

This plan isn't a cure, and it isn't a substitute for a doctor, a licensed counselor, a pastor, a treatment program, or the real people who will walk with you. It's meant to go alongside treatment and those people, never in place of them. I'm a pastor, not a physician, and nothing here is medical advice. If you drink or use every day, don't stop suddenly on your own, because stopping alcohol and some other drugs can be dangerous. If anyone has taken too much and can't be woken or is barely breathing, call 911, and if drinking or using has brought you to thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988 now. Walk the plan imperfectly. A missed week is not failure; you just pick it back up.
careNote: These weeks walk beside a doctor, a licensed counselor, and the people helping you, never in place of them, and if you drink or use every day, see a doctor before you stop. If someone can't be woken or is barely breathing, call 911; for treatment, SAMHSA's helpline is on the Find Help page; and in a crisis, call or text 988.

weeks.focus: Stopping safely, starting with a doctor
weeks.why: You've tried to quit on your own before, maybe more than once, and tonight you may want to try again. Hear this first, plainly: if you drink or use every day, don't stop suddenly by yourself, because stopping alcohol and some other drugs can be dangerous. Withdrawal from alcohol or some prescription sedatives can bring on seizures and become life-threatening. The first faithful step, then, is a phone call, to a doctor or to SAMHSA's National Helpline on the Find Help page, so that you stop with medical help. Asking for that help takes nothing away from your faith. God has always cared for bodies through ordinary means, and doctors are among them. And if anyone has taken too much and can't be woken or is barely breathing, call 911 at once.
weeks.practice: Each day, write one honest line: what you drank or used, about how much, and when. Early this week, not at its end, call your doctor or SAMHSA's helpline from the Find Help page. Say plainly that you're drinking or using more than you can control and need help stopping safely, then read them your lines and every medicine you take. If you're pregnant, tell them that first.

read.label: I can't stop drinking or using, the care page, with how to stop safely and where treatment starts

tool.label: The Find Help page, where SAMHSA's National Helpline is listed with 988 and 911

weeks.reflection: What has kept me from telling a doctor the whole truth, and is that reason worth what it's costing me?

weeks.focus: Telling one person the whole truth
weeks.why: In Romans 7, Paul speaks in the first person of a self at war with itself: "I do not understand what I do. For what I want to do, I do not do. But what I hate, I do" (Romans 7:15). He wasn't writing about addiction, but anyone who has made the same promise every morning and broken it by night knows that voice. Notice where his question goes: he doesn't ask how to fix himself, but "Who will rescue me from this body of death?" (Romans 7:24), and the answer he gives is a person. You can't be rescued from what you insist you control, which is why the way out begins with the truth told to someone else. You don't need everyone to know, only one person who knows all of it.
weeks.practice: Choose one person who will keep your confidence and won't shield you from the consequences: a friend who won't flinch, a pastor, a counselor, or your doctor. Each day, pray for that person by name and for the nerve to speak. Before the week ends, tell them how much, how often, and for how long, and ask them to check on you once a week.

read.label: When You Are Trapped by Addiction, on the chains willpower can't break and the truth told to one safe person

tool.label: The Prayer Generator's prayers before a hard conversation, for the day you tell them

weeks.reflection: What part of the truth have I never said out loud, and who is one person who could hear all of it?

weeks.why: Look back at the times your resolve broke, and you may find that it keeps a schedule: the quiet hour at the end of the day, alone; the drive home past the store; a certain friend's house; the evening after a hard phone call. Proverbs sketches a drinker who was beaten and never felt it, and whose first thought is the next one: "When can I wake up to search for another drink?" (Proverbs 23:35). The craving plans ahead, so you'll need to plan too. Paul assured the Corinthians that God "will also provide an escape" (1 Corinthians 10:13), and his next sentence tells them to flee. The word you in that promise is plural in Greek, spoken to a church, so the way out is often a person to call or a road home that doesn't pass the store.
weeks.practice: Write down your hardest hour and your riskiest places. Each day, give that hour a different shape: take another route home, eat with someone, walk, or call the person you told. Put that person's number at the top of your phone. Once a doctor has helped you plan to stop safely, clear what's left out of the house, with someone beside you if that helps. If any of it was prescribed, ask the prescriber first.

read.label: How Do You Fight Temptation and Disordered Desire? On naming your weakest hours and guarding the worst one

tool.label: The Verse Finder's Temptation verses, 1 Corinthians 10:13 and Hebrews 4:15-16 among them

weeks.reflection: When and where does my resolve usually break, and what would it take for me to be somewhere else at that hour?

weeks.why: After the first sin, the man and woman hid, and when God called to him, the man answered, "I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself" (Genesis 3:10). Addiction runs on that reflex: the bottle behind the paint cans, the receipts thrown away, the story rehearsed on the drive home. Shame and use feed each other, because hiding makes you want relief and the relief gives you more to hide. The church has too often tightened the loop by treating the person who drinks or uses as the worst sinner in the building, and I'm a pastor, so I'm inside that failure. Look at what God did in the garden. He came looking and asked, "Where are you?" (Genesis 3:9), and before they left he made them garments and clothed them (Genesis 3:21).
weeks.practice: Each day, write down one thing you've hidden or one story you've told to cover it. Don't punish yourself with the list. Before the week ends, read it to the person you told in week two. If you drink or use again during these weeks, it isn't the end of the road; tell them that same day and call your doctor. With opioids, tolerance drops after time away, and your old amount can cause an overdose.

read.label: What Is the Difference Between Guilt and Shame? On the self that has been hiding since Eden

tool.label: Genesis 3 in the Study Bible, the hiding and the garments God made, with notes on the chapter

weeks.reflection: If God asked me where I am, as he asked the man in the garden, what would I honestly answer?

weeks.why: Somewhere underneath, the substance has been doing a job. It may quiet anxiety, grief, an old wound, loneliness, boredom, or a marriage gone cold, and for an hour it works, which is the trap. In Isaiah, God calls to people who have spent themselves on what can't feed them: "Why spend money on that which is not bread, and your labor on that which does not satisfy?" (Isaiah 55:2). The hunger was real, and they were feeding it with something that was never bread. Naming what you've been quieting doesn't excuse anything. It shows you the need that will still be there when the substance is gone, so that God and people can meet it. Where the wound is deep, trauma or depression among them, a licensed counselor is part of that help.
weeks.practice: Each day, when the craving comes, stop long enough to name in one word what you want it to quiet: tired, afraid, lonely, angry, ashamed, bored, grieving. Write the word down. Then do one small thing that answers the real need: eat, rest, call someone, or pray one honest sentence. At the week's end, show the list to a counselor, or ask your doctor for the name of one.

read.label: Why Can't Willpower Alone Break an Addiction? On the captive will and the deeper wounds beneath it

tool.label: The Emotional Health Self-Check, fifteen questions on self-awareness, grief, and rest, a mirror and not a diagnosis

weeks.reflection: What does the drink or the drug quiet in me for an hour, and who could help me face that without it?

weeks.why: The letter of James places confession among ordinary believers: "Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed" (James 5:16). Both verbs run both ways, so the people who hear your confession are also people you pray for. Too many churches have said, in effect, get clean first and then come back, which is the kind of yoke Paul warned the Galatians against when religious people added requirements to grace (Galatians 5:1). Jesus came eating and drinking, and his critics called him a "glutton and drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners" (Matthew 11:19). We in the church have often feared that accusation more than he did. You need rooms where confession can happen: a recovery group of people who know this from the inside, and a church that receives people as they are.
weeks.practice: Go to one recovery meeting this week, in person or online, through a church recovery ministry or another group, and sit in the back; you don't have to say a word. If it isn't a fit, try another, and if you're in a treatment program, its group counts. Each day, pray by name for the person you told and for one person you met there, and confess one specific thing to God in plain words.

read.label: Why Christians Confess Their Sins Out Loud, on why a secret loses its power when it's spoken to someone who doesn't run

tool.label: The Prayer Planner, to give each person walking with you a day in your prayers

weeks.reflection: Where could I be known as I really am, and what has kept me from walking into that room?

weeks.why: Addiction lives in the body, and so does the long work of getting free. A body that has carried a substance for a long time needs time, and when sleep won't come or the evenings are hard, the doctor helping you is the one to tell. Scripture is gentle with bodies: "As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him. For He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust" (Psalm 103:13-14). Regular sleep, real meals, daylight, and movement sound too plain to matter, but a body mends through plain days repeated. And if a doctor prescribes medicine for this, taking it isn't a failure of faith.
weeks.practice: Each day, keep the same bedtime and waking time, eat three real meals, and walk outside in daylight for fifteen minutes. Give your phone a bedtime an hour before yours. Keep every appointment with your doctor and counselor, and take any medicine prescribed for this exactly as prescribed. If sleep won't come, tell your doctor instead of reaching for something on your own.

read.label: How to Sleep Like a Creature Who Trusts God, on a set bedtime, a phone outside the bedroom, and a doctor when sleep won't come

tool.label: The Worry Journal, five minutes before bed to name what's pressing, the one thing to do tomorrow, and a prayer

weeks.reflection: How have I been treating my body, and what would it look like to treat it as something God is mindful of?

weeks.why: Stopping leaves an empty hour, and an empty hour asks to be filled. The letter to the Ephesians, after warning against drunkenness, doesn't end with the warning: "Instead, be filled with the Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18), and the filling it describes is a people speaking psalms to one another, singing, and giving thanks (Ephesians 5:19-20). Paul told the Galatians they were called to freedom, then said what freedom is for: "serve one another in love" (Galatians 5:13). A life with something to live toward is built from ordinary things: a table, work done well, a friend who knows the truth, someone who needs what you've learned. Some of it will be repair, making right what you can with people you've hurt, with a counselor's or pastor's help and without pressing anyone who isn't ready. The road is longer than eight weeks, and it was never meant to be walked alone.
weeks.practice: Write on a card the two or three practices from these weeks that held you, with when and where you'll keep them. Add one thing to live toward: a person to serve, a skill to learn, a table to sit at each week. Show the card to the person you told, and keep your treatment and your group alongside it, not instead of them.

read.label: Serving Others, on finding the need nearest you and meeting it without announcement

tool.label: The Rule of Life Builder, to choose a bedtime, weekly worship, one friend who knows the truth about you, and a hidden act of service

weeks.reflection: What do I want my evenings to hold a year from now, and who will I ask to help me keep it?
